Messages.Body:
Here's some fun house errata for RTI which, in my opinion, balances the card
and still makes it fun to play with. The idea is that the vampire becomes
human at the beginning of the action rather than at the end.

(D) bleed your prey with +X bleed where X is the capacity of the acting
vampire. The acting vampire may not play cards requiring disciplines during
this action. Remove this vampire from the game after the action's conclusion.

Basically this idea increases the risk and greatly decreases the unblockability
of RTI, and still lets it have a play combo by using the Concoction of
Vitality. It only adds to the existing text and doesn't seem too complicated to
me. It may stillrestrict the card too much and still make it wallpaper, but hey
so does 7/7. please let me know what you all think about this. Does it create
balance and continue to be powerful enough to have fun with? Is it too
complicated? Does it wallpaper the card? I really would like to know.

Return To Innocence:
Cost: 0
Disp/clan: Pander or Catiff
Card Text: Unblockable. (D) Bleed for X+1. Return this vampire to your

which you can do easily with presence or Dominate. And if you want more, you
have to slap disp. masters on your vamps, which will take you time and will

Like I said, I was only thinking, but what do people think? Would it be at al

Well, yes, because Return to Innocence is an inherently unbalanced
card concept. Therefore, anything that adheres to its design will
tend to still be overpowered.

Making it harder to make RtI unblockable certainly makes it *less*
overpowered. But the huge pool loss that can be inflicted in a single
action makes RtI too close to the hypothetical 'D Action: Oust your
prey' card.

(Even the 7/7 version of RtI isn't exactly fixed; again it's been
weakened, but it still causes a very large pool loss from one action,
if it succeeds.)

I'm agreeable to adding 'this vampire can't play cards until the action
has resolved' to RtI's original text, but I can't say that it actually
goes far enough to make the card balanced. Nothing that says
'Bleed at +X, where X is the vamp's capacity' can be very effectively
balanced as long as it says that. (As others have pointed out, there
aren't even any bleed-discipline cards that give bonuses this large.
So it seems unreasonable for a disciplineless card to be able to
do it.)

Part of the problem here, of course, is that I don't think RtI was
ever 'fun to play with.' About as fun as Fireballing your opponent
for 20, as far as I can see.

Josh

CPilh...@bhak12.ac.at wrote:

: Then why isn't it fixed with "Bleed at +X, where X is the vamps's capacity

: halfed down, rounded up."? Sounds pretty simple to me if only the +X bleed
: concerns you.

Well, that would certainly make it closer to balanced. With rounding
up, it would only be 3 times as effective as Govern the Unaligned for
an IC member (+6 bleed) and twice as effective for a 7/8-cap vamp (+4
bleed).

: However, I don't think that the card is broken if no cards whatsoever can

: be played until the action is concluded. This means, the action is not
: unblockable, is not at stealth, and cannot be pushed by further bleed
: modifiers. If the action is successful the vamp is still burnt, but it
: wouldn't circumvent the costs for DayOp or Daring the Dawn! And if a player
: makes a tactical mistake and gets tapped out before his predator gets in
: for the kill with RtI, then it's that players fault, the card can't be
: blamed. It's really easy to defend against RtI if it is not at stealth or
: unblockable.

Sure the card can be blamed. It's an action card requiring no disciplines,
requiring no other cards to combo with it to produce its large game-
swinging effect. Someone can pull out RtI as the only +bleed card in
their deck, after spending the entire beginning of the game calling
votes that you can't block (because you're not playing an intercept
deck). It's hard to say it was a tactical mistake to be tapped out
in such a case.

: I think the main concerns were the unblockable combos, the proposed fix would

: remove that abuse. Also, burning a stolen vamp with RtI is also a lot more
: difficult as the action is easily blocked.

: Additionally, the "fixed" RtI is also a valuable card for Bruise&Bleed
: decks (block me or it'll hurt!).

RtI has always been a more valuable card for decks that try to abuse
it than 'normal' decks. A bruise&bleed deck usually wants to be able
to keep taking actions with several vampires each turn. Burning a
vamp for one large bleed is probably not as useful as keeping the vamp
around to do several smaller bleeds, for a bruise&bleed deck.

So, due to the high cost (especially the burning a vamp part) and
huge effect of RtI, I think it's very dubious that it can ever be
balanced while remaining anything close to faithful to its original
text or intent. As it was written, the card demands to be abused,
or else not used at all.

: You may be right, that the card with it's original text is way to

: powerful. But with the fix proposed, it is by no means devastating.
: Simply block the action. That's what the fix is for. No more
: unblockable oust-combos.

Certainly the no-action-mods fix makes it *less* powerful. But
nothing that allows such a massive bleed can avoid being *excessively*
powerful. Consider Misdirection, RtI. To avoid that, you need to
be playing a deck with Wakes (or Sudden Reversals). The problem is
that RtI's bleed is just *too big*. As long as it's so large, it
can't help being too close to "D: Oust your prey", as far as I'm
concerned.

Josh

: Bah, Misdirection is always a problem if you have no Wakes. A normal
: bleed deck (like Tremere) tap you and bleed at will. You're out of the
: game nonetheless. It just takes 2 vamps instead of one, and they are
: still there after you are ousted. So what?

: Sure the card IS useful, but it can be dealt with.

Well, in my opinion, Misdirection is only a problem if there are
actions that are overpowered. For many decks in many cases,
Misdirection is relatively irrelevant because either they'll be
tapping out every turn to take the actions that the deck is based
on (Bum's Rush, Bleeds, Votes, whatever) or else it's a deck
intended to block a lot, in which case it probably has substantial
untaps. The only time Misdirection ends up hurting a lot is if
the deck either relies on leaving minions untapped to block (a weenie
deck without untaps, for example) or if the untappy-deck happens not
to have untaps at the right time.

My example of Misdirection here was intended just to point out that
the 'there's always a defense if the action is always blockable,
because you can just block' is not a very useful defense for a lot
of decks. Decks that tap out every turn to take actions are fairly
common in my experience. They don't necessarily want (in general)
to leave vamps untapped for blocking, because the vamps will be
less effective as blockers than as actors.

If RtI makes it necessary for every deck to leave vamps untapped
to block, because it'll still oust you if it gets through, even if
it can't be made unblockable, it's still having an unacceptable
impact on the game. (I think this is less likely to happen with
RtI as +X/2 rather than +X. I just can't reiterate enough that
the whole idea of a disciplineless card that produces the biggest
bleed in the game is dubious at best.)

Josh

Return to Innocence could pay 2 pool to cancel the bleed? Thus, you wouldn't
end up paying the high cost, etc. You might look at this and say, "well
duh... of course they'll pay, that's useless." But, let's compare it to
Computer Hacking, shall we?

Assuming that the 2 pool will be paid every time... Computer Hacking will
result in a bleed for 2, this may be modified by other bleed cards, but may
be lowered with Telepathic Counter and that one Chimerstry card. Further,
you can get Major Booned by your predator, always a bad thing when it
happens. It will also get you the Edge. This version of Return to Innocence
will cause a loss of 2 pool which may not be modified by other bleed cards
and may not be Telepathically Countered or Major Booned. If you're not
playing a bleed discipline, this version seems just slightly better than
Computer Hacking (if the 2 pool is always paid). If you *are* playing a
bleed discipline, get some balls and use a real (D)bleed card; don't bother
with Computer Hacking or RtI.

If the 2 pool is not paid, you end up bleeding for a bunch and losing a vamp.
This would make it a risky proposition to use RtI with a 4 cap (your prey
might just take the bleed for 5, and make you lose your vampire), but if you
have the right cards in your hand, you may be able to psyche your prey into
taking a big bleed, while you have the capacity to benefit (Possession,
Redeem the Lost Soul, etc...). And the best part... this adds very little
text to the original and still has the same general mechanics. Alternately,
perhaps make the player pay 3 pool to cancel the bleed instead of 2.

In case anyone gets confused, we're talking about the following proposed
RTI fix: Add the line "If this action remains unblocked, your predator
may pay 2 pool to cause this action to fail."

On 12 Aug 1998, Jasper Phillips wrote:

> >It is in the most "abusive" situations, (such as an ousting bleed for 17
> >with an IC member) that the predator is most likely to take the 2 pool
> >burn option.
>
> Well, I won't argue that it can't be usefull, but if it's only usefull
> in the situations you describe it still looks like wallpaper to me
> (the only really viable possibility being if your predator has <=2 pool.
> You may as well just ban the card.

I think you are so familiar with how RTI was normally played, that you
have given no thought to how it *would* be played if this fix were
adopted.

There are lots of reasons why your predator would agree to let the RTI go
through. One of them is, of course, that stopping it costs 2 pool.
Another reason is that a successful RTI gives your predator something he
wants: the destruction of one of your vampires. The destruction of a
vampire is a high cost to pay. So I play RTI saying to my predator "I
have damaged my prey, but I'm also damaging myself as well, which is
something *you* want."

The problem with old RTI is that high cost (destruction of a vampire) is
easily circumvented by a number of ways:

1) One means of circumventing this cost was that old RTI was *never* used
unless the action would oust prey if successful. It made less sense to
use the card at other times, so it was always saved until preys pool was
low enough. But when it was used to oust prey, the destruction of your
own vampire was repaid by the gaining of 6 pool, (which could be used to
bring out another vampire). It was never used when prey had enough pool
to take the bleed, since the cost would not thereby be circumvented.
With the above fix, however, the ousting will not meet the
approval of my predator, who will stop it if he can. Thus, I am not
likely to try that tactic. I am far more likely to attempt RTI bleeds
that will leave my prey standing. In doing so, I take a risk, since I do
not directly oust my prey, and have damaged myself. You see the
difference? Destruction of one of my vampires in exchange for significant
pool loss for my prey can be a fair exchange (and my predator might
actually think this is to his benefit). Destruction of a vampire in
exchange for destruction of a Methuselah is NOT fair. You directly gain a
victory point AND 6 pool. No vampire is worth that much.

2) Another way of circumventing the cost of RTI was by means of Minion
Tap. The bigger the vampire, the greater the portion of his cost you can
recover before using RTI. You spend 11 to bring him out, but then you
Minion Tap to recover 6, recovering half his cost before destroying him.
This meant that RTI was always used with the biggest vampires possible.
No-one played RTI with 4 capacity vampires, since the entire cost of the
vampire always had to be sacrificed.
This would change with the above fix, because if I go too far to
circumvent the cost, then my predator has no reason to allow it to happen.
On the other hand, I could bring out my IC member, with him still at
capacity, have him bleed for +11, severely damaging my prey, but not
immediately ousting him. Should my predator pay 2 pool to stop me? Why?
I have paid 11 pool to do +11 damage to my prey, so I have arguably
damaged myself just as much as he. If my predator feels he has a good
chance of finishing me off before I finish off my prey, then he has no
reason to stop me. Also, if I play RTI with a 4 capacity minion, why
would my predator want to pay 2 pool to save my minion and restore 5 pool
to some other methuselah (unless the move would oust my prey and gain me
6)?

3) A third way of circumventing the cost of RTI is by using it to
circumvent the cost of another card: Day Operation. Day Operation is a
powerful card with a serious cost, but that serious cost was meaningless
when used with (old) RTI.
With the above fix, this cost cannot be circumvented. Playing RTI
with Day Operation merely gives your predator the opportunity to pay 2
pool to send your vampire to torpor tapped, while still causing your
action to fail.

4) A fourth way of circumventing the cost of RTI is by means of the Soul
Gem of Etrius, which gets you a younger vampire, filled to capacity, in
exchange for the one you destroyed, thus offsetting the cost by up to 10
blood points.
This will no longer work, as predator has no reason to agree.

So you see, one can still bleed with RTI with the proposed fix, but only
so long as one does not use the usual tactics to circumvent the cost. If
a 12 capacity IC member, minion tapped to 6 pool, with a soul gem plays
RTI with conditioning and Day Operation for 18 bleed to his prey, ousting
him because he has only 17, gaining 6 pool, a victory point, and a brand
new IC member filled to capacity who will be Minion Tapped next
turn...well, of course my predator will willingly pay 2 pool to stop that
AS WELL HE SHOULD.

However if I do not try these abusive tactics, my RTI can indeed be more
than just a back bleed for 2. The trick is doing it in such a manner as
to make it LOOK to my predator that I am damaging myself almost as much as
my prey. Of course, I still might think I know better, cause he doesn't
know what cards I have. Then again, he might think he knows better than
me because I don't know what cards he has (such as maybe a Pentex
Subversion and plenty of bum's rush and combat cards to take out my few
remaining vampires and leave me at his mercy). This aspect would exist
even if cancelling the RTI cost only one pool...or even nothing at all.

Indeed, the proposed fix has the potential to turn this tedious card into
something somewhat interesting.

Your predator doesn't have to just "not mind". He has to not mind enough
to pay 2 pool to stop you. As a clanless, disciplineless bleed card, RTI
should be no more powerful than, say, computer hacking.

Would you pay 2 pool to cause a computer hacking action to fail? I doubt
it. Even though it is of benefit to your prey in helping to oust HIS
prey, it is not enough of a benefit to him that you would choose to take
the pool loss INSTEAD of his prey. I doubt you would pay 2 pool for most
predator actions.

If you use RTI in such a manner that it causes you no more benefit than
Computer Hacking -- such that it brings you closer to death by x, and your
prey closer to death by x+2 -- then it still will not be worth it to your
prey to burn 2 pool to stop you.

I can still see it being a very powerful underdog card -- used to knock a
giant down to size. When you get to a three player game, this can be a
benefit to both you AND your predator, as you will be damaging his
predator, and taking the pressure off him.

If you put one in a deck, there is no guarantee that you will be able to
use it. But if you do use it, you might well do so to great effect.

> I understand exactly what it does, but I would rather have standard
> bleed cards that will actually help me when I'm doing well. IMHO,
> despite the points you make, such RtI would be wallpaper.

Perhaps, but that for you would be no loss, in any case, since it was
forbidden in your playgroup.

When 2 players remain, the action, if successful, will cause 2 pool loss
per action. It will be just as good as Computer Hacking in such
circumstances, unless you do it with Beast and your prey decides it's
worth an extra 6 pool to get rid of him.

There may be something wrong with my analysis, but I suspect that, when
there are more than 2 players remaining, the card is still at least as
good as Computer Hacking, though analysis here becomes more difficult.

The concept originally presented by LSJ, derived from the Golconda
analogy, was that it was your prey who would have the option to burn 2
pool. This version makes it even more likely to be stopped, and it is
clearly balanced compared to computer hacking, but ends up seeming like a
glorified version of it.

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
When considering whether cards are overpowered/underpowered, it is often
useful to compare them to baseline cards like Majesty, Lucky Blow, KRC,
and Computer Hacking. Everyone agrees (hopefully) that these cards are
the epitome of balance and fairness in the game. So, let's compare RtI
to CH:

Computer Hacking
Blood Cost: zero
Opportunity Cost: zero
Effect: +1 bleed

Return to Innocence
Blood Cost: four
Opportunity Cost: vampire burns if successful
Effect: +X bleed, X >= 4 due to blood cost

[I might be using the term "opportunity cost" incorrectly; I mean this
to be the cost in terms of future opportunities; RtI's burning of the
vampire keeps you from having future possbile actions]

So RtI has a greatly increased cost, and a greatly increased effect.
Since its cost is so high, people have argued that the huge effect the
card has is balanced. It is true that the "abuses" discussed in concert
with RtI -- unblockability, high stealth, etc. -- can be used with
Computer Hacking, but with RtI, the effect of the single action is so
much higher that the benefits of such "abuses" are greatly increased.

When is it worthwhile to play RtI? The effect, +X bleed, at first
glance seems to be offset by the burn cost; your prey has lost X pool,
and you have lost X pool in the form of an X-capacity vampire. But, as
anyone who has played a combat deck knows, destroying an X-capacity
vampire is not the same as bleeding a player for X pool. First of all,
the amount of blood on the vampire is fluid, and has not necessarily all
come from the player's pool but rather from cards like Art Museum or
Tomb of Ramses III. Also, the vampire's blood can have been moved into
the players pool by way of Minion Tap or Blood Doll, among other
things. If a deck is designed to take advantage of RtI, the vampire's
cost will likely have been recovered by the time the action is taken.
Secondly, the loss of X pool in a single is often devestating, most
often to the point of ousting the recipient, thus providing the ousting
player with 6 pool, which also serves to offset the card's high cost.
Take into account the abuses possible with Soul Gem, and the card has a
negative cost; it bleeds your prey for X, likely ousts him, gaining you
6 pool and a victory point, and you get a free vampire, full of blood
and ready to repeat the process. The success of this strategy is not in
dispute; decks of this nature (until 7/7) won tournaments handily.

What about the supposed drawbacks of RtI? Like any bleed, this one can
be deflected, to devestating effect. But since not every deck can use
this defense, this hardly justifies RtI's power. The action can also be
made unblockable very easily, with Fortitude, Protean, or simply with
equipment. In a deck that cannot guarantee the success and
cost-effectiveness of the action, with the above methods, RtI's cost is
simply too high; no one wants to risk their vampire for an action that
can easily fail disastrously. So no one will play with this card unless
it is to abuse it. Hence RtI is alternatively wallpaper and the most
powerful card in the game.

----------------------

All of that said, what of the "your predator can burn 2 pool to make
this action fail" clause? I really don't like this "fix", since it
really doesn't fix the card. It's just as abusive, but if your predator
is in a magnanimous mood, they will spare your prey's life. But this
leaves too much up to the whimsy of people at the table, and doesn't get
to the heart of what's wrong with this card: it's simply too much to
have a card provide +X bleed, where X ranges as high as 11. The card
just screams out to be abused. If you add more and more restrictions on
the card, it will still oscillate between extremes; in the few instances
when the action is successful, it is just as devestating. It encourages
people not to use the card by making it less versatile, but RtI is still
a huge sledgehammer. By making it heavier and heavier you make it
harder to lift, but when someone manages to, it's just as deadly.

Ah, here is where we make an interesting digression from the beaten
path. To whit:

A) Most arguements on RTI focus on it's unbalanced nature as a single
card action (usually blended and pureed with Day Ops).

B) My arguement contends that as a deck strategy, in the context of
predator and prey relationships, RTI (in combo with Day Ops or huge
stealth/Elder Imp.) is far from overpowered.

Now, let me make a some of points here:

1) As a single combo, RTI/Day Ops, especially when using RTI as it was
printed, is a killer combo. Almost, as many say, the prototypical
"oust your prey" card. However....see 2)

2) It is the extended combo's that make RTI truly game unbalancing
as I see it.
a) RTI/Day Ops/Soul Gem
b) Tomb/RTI/Day Ops
c) Mind Rape/RTI/Day Ops

The deck mentioned above was an effective deck. When it rolled, it
really rolled. However, it did not make use of any of the three
items mentioned above, or any other combo extension that boosts the
inherent power of RTI/Day Ops.

To re-iterate the point. You could build any RTI/Day Ops deck, and
if it doesn't use any of the combo extensions above, you would be
at the mercy of your predator - just as any other deck in the game
is. Combat or Vote or Bleed or whatever combination, a reasonably
effective predator that puts pressure on you (the prey) will disrupt
your RTI strategy and you will be ousted. You may take out your
initial prey, you may not. You may clear the table, you may not.
Your VP totals with that deck will not be any greater than anyone
else in your playgroup that uses a decent deck.

Until, of course, you extend your combo. At this point the balance
of predator/prey comes into question. (In my own lunatic mind
anyways) RTI, as is, provides a big bang for the buck - with those
other cards - ouch.

For this reason you have to look at all the cards as a group.

RTI - reduce the maximum 'real' bleed possible, whether you go
with my "max X bleed" concept or the "+X/2"
concept, pick one. I do not view 7/7 as acceptable.

Tomb - bring the 'cost reduction' aspect of the card into line,
I personally like the Tomb counters idea

Mind Rape - don't really know what to do here, perhaps I'll read
7/7 again. Who knows? Maybe there will be a ruling,
besides the Thoughts Betrayed ruling, that I liked.

Soul Gem - maybe it should cost 2 pool, like the V:TES version says.
Or maybe, with the RTI in line, a 0 pool cost is OK.
Don't know.

Wow, am I ever drifting here (sorry). Regardless, like any other
deck being played, a basic RTI deck is at the mercy of card draw
and table seating like any other.

I can see your point, that as a single card action RTI (as written)
may be overbalancing. I hope you can see mine, that as a 'deck
strategy' RTI (in and of itself) is no better or worse than many
others. When brought into combination with other cards though, more
than just Day Ops, RTI threatens table balance - and that is something
I would like to see balanced more than taking the easy way out and
neutering the card.

Hoping I almost sound intelligent, yet not holding my breath....

This is a good fix, but I think a lot of people would question whether it
goes far enough. One might say that the main problem with RTI is not that
it gains you pool, but that it wins the game for you, and loses it for
someone else. The victory point you gain may be so significant that your
pool count becomes irrelevant. Even if playing RTI does not leave you with
enough resources to survive, the victory point you gain can be of immense
significance, especially in tournament play where you might otherwise have
gained *no* victory points. For your victem, the significance of this
action is absolute.

Your fix would have no significance in the end game, where only 2 players
remain. If you already have 2 victory points, then one more will
typically win you the game, even if your are subsequently ousted. With 1
victory point already, one more is often enough for a tie game. In
tournament games, which are so often called on time, 2 victory points is
often enough to make you the top player at the table.

I think any fix of RTI must address the issue of ensuring that the cards
cost--the loss of a vampire--remains significant after the action
resolves. But the only reason you need the vampire in the first place is
to help you win the game. If the action gains you victory or partial
victory (as the unfixed version almost always does) then the sacrifice of
this vampire involves no real risk. He has already served his purpose.

With RTI, the cost might be appropriate to the effect only if your prey
really does have enough pool to take the bleed. For instance: If my prey
has 15 pool, and I RTI him for 10 with a 9 capacity minion, leaving him at
5 pool and me without my biggest minion, I bring him closer to death but
also take a serious risk to myself. I have not won the game yet and since
I have lost one of the minions I need to win the game the sacrifice I made
for the enormous bleed was not meaningless. I believe if the use of RTI
were somehow restricted to circumstances like the above, then it would be
a balanced card.

I can think of no truly elegant fixes that would ensure this. One idea is
my previous suggestion (predator may burn 2 pool to cause action to fail),
which ensures that action will be cancelled any time is used for
"overwhelming" benefit (which would probably include any time it is used
to oust). However, there is no guarantee that a predator would be willing
to pay two pool to stop an oust (especially if it's the only 2 pool he has
left).

Other thoughts:

"Only usable when your prey has 2x pool or more." [x, if you recall, is
the capacity of the acting minion.]

"If this action would oust your prey, he instead withdraws instantly with
one victory point."
